nodes.title: How the whitespace works
nodes.summary: Start here: the parts of the whitespace and how they fit, with guided tours in the panel's tour menu.
nodes.text:
# How the whitespace works

A *space* is a JSON file of objects (notes, code, files, 3D plots) and links. The viewer (**src/main.js**) lays them out in 3D with three.js and lets you fly around, read, search and run code.

- **Objects and faces**: each object is a slab whose face is a texture drawn on a canvas; semantic zoom shows less from afar and more up close.
- **Running code**: Sagebrush's own engine, in the browser (**src/run.js**).
- **The agents chat**: the agent writes a `.space.json`; the chat page shows it in a frame and writes your selection back into the file.
- **VR**: **src/xr.js** puts the same space in a headset, with controllers, a reading panel and a wrist menu.

This space is made by **gen-self.mjs** from the code itself, so it is always current. Pick a tour in the panel to follow one path through it.

nodes.title: main.js · the scene
nodes.summary: Sets up the 3D world: the WebGL renderer, the scene, the camera and its orbit controls, the lights, and the colour themes (light by default, dark, or following the system).

nodes.title: main.js · faces and textures
nodes.summary: Draws what you read on each slab. A face is a canvas painted with the title, the summary, the first lines of text or code, and the output, then used as a texture. A plot's surface becomes a mesh coloured by height. Math is drawn as readable text (tex.js).

nodes.title: main.js · objects and their shapes
nodes.summary: Makes the 3D object for each item: a slab sized by kind (a file's grows with its length), a small shape above it chosen by the item's id, and, for a plot, the 3D plot standing on its face.

nodes.title: main.js · semantic zoom
nodes.summary: Semantic zoom: far away a slab is a plain block in its group's colour, nearer it shows its title and summary, close up its whole face. Textures are made lazily, the nearest first, a few per frame.

nodes.title: main.js · group labels
nodes.summary: The big labels above each group (a directory, a crate, a topic), placed over the group and faded in as you leave it. Each frame, labels that would overlap on screen are hidden, the biggest groups first.

nodes.title: main.js · loading and framing
nodes.summary: Loads a space: checks its format, makes the objects and the links between them, lays them out (saved positions, or a force layout), builds the search index, and frames the camera on everything.

nodes.title: main.js · flying, Back, Forward
nodes.summary: Moves the camera. Flying to an object goes to the view in front of its face (or below and in front of a plot), along an arc over the space. Every flight is remembered, for Back and Forward.

nodes.title: main.js · picking
nodes.summary: Turns the mouse into objects: a ray from the camera through the pointer finds what is under it. Hovering lights it up; a click (not a drag) opens it in the drawer.

nodes.title: main.js · selection (for agents)
nodes.summary: What the person is looking at, for agents: the selected object goes into the address (#sel=), window.whitespace.selection, an event, and a message to the page around it, which writes it into the file as "selected".

nodes.title: main.js · guided tours
nodes.summary: Guided tours: a list of stops, each an object and some narration. A tour flies from stop to stop; the drawer shows the stop with Back, Next and End (keys N and P), and the headset shows it on the panel.

nodes.title: main.js · running code
nodes.summary: Runs an object's code on Sagebrush's engine in the browser (run.js). The output, figures and 3D plots are kept on the object and drawn on its face; a Sage 3D plot replaces the object's shape. Run all runs every object in order.

nodes.title: main.js · what this browser keeps
nodes.summary: Keeps what you edited and ran in this browser (localStorage), each copy tagged with the file text it came from, so the agent's next version of an object always wins over an old copy.

nodes.title: main.js · panel, theme, keys
nodes.summary: The drawer's width (drag its edge), the light/dark theme switch, full screen, and flying with the keyboard (W A S D or arrows, E and Q up and down, Shift for speed).

nodes.title: main.js · search
nodes.summary: Full-text search over titles, summaries, text and output. The best matches first; click one to fly there.

nodes.title: main.js · which space; embedding
nodes.summary: Picks the space to show: from the list of example spaces, or, embedded in the agents chat (?embed=1), from messages the page sends each time the agent writes the file.

nodes.title: main.js · the headset hookup
nodes.summary: Connects the headset mode (xr.js): the Enter VR and Enter AR buttons, what it may call back (select, run, fly to an object, tours), and the animation loop shared by the screen and the headset.

nodes.title: xr.js · setup and the rig
nodes.summary: The headset mode, built on WebXR: the rig that carries the camera (scaled so a slab is about a metre wide) and the reference space with its floor.

nodes.title: xr.js · controllers
nodes.summary: A ray from each controller, drawn as a line that stops at whatever it points at.

nodes.title: xr.js · flying in VR
nodes.summary: Flying in VR: to an object's view (the same view the desktop flies to), smoothly, and Back, Forward and See all, each flight remembered.

nodes.title: xr.js · the reading panel
nodes.summary: The reading panel: a canvas texture floating beside the object, with the title, summary, tour narration, code and output, and buttons (Run, scroll, Next stop, Close), because a page's own HTML isn't drawn inside a headset.

nodes.title: xr.js · the wrist menu
nodes.summary: The menu on the left wrist: Back, Forward, See all, Run all, Tour or Next stop, and Exit VR.

nodes.title: xr.js · pointing and selecting
nodes.summary: Pointing and pulling the trigger: a hit on the panel or the menu presses its button; a hit on an object flies there and opens it.

nodes.title: xr.js · each frame: rays and thumbsticks
nodes.summary: Each frame: the rays and what they hover, the thumbsticks (move, rise and fall, turn in steps; the grip for speed), and B or Y for Back.

nodes.title: xr.js · entering and leaving
nodes.summary: Entering VR or AR (in AR the background goes, so the room shows) and leaving: the camera goes back where it was.

nodes.title: src/run.js
nodes.summary: Runs code on Sagebrush's engine in a Web Worker, one engine per language (so MATLAB can't see Sage's names), and turns a Sage 3D scene into three.js objects.

nodes.title: src/code.js
nodes.summary: Syntax highlighting (highlight.js) and the small code editor in the drawer: a textarea over a highlighted copy; Shift+Enter runs.

nodes.title: src/layout.js
nodes.summary: The force layout: links pull objects together, everything pushes everything else apart, and groups gather around their centre. Fixed positions stay put; `near` puts an object beside another.

nodes.title: src/tex.js
nodes.summary: TeX as plain text for canvases, where KaTeX can't draw: $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ becomes 4/3 π r³. Used on faces and the VR panel; the drawer typesets the real thing.

nodes.title: index.html
nodes.summary: The page: the panel (title, Back, Forward, See all, Flatten, Full screen, Run all, Theme, tours, search), the drawer, and all the styles, with the light and dark colours as variables.
nodes.text:
Whitespace
    Whitespace · rough alpha
    Drag to turn · scroll to move closer · right-drag to pan · W A S D / arrows, E Q: fly (Shift: faster) · click an object to read it · B / F: back, forward · H: see all · /: search

nodes.title: build.mjs
nodes.summary: Bundles src/main.js with esbuild into space.js (three.js inside, nothing fetched from other sites) and copies the page and example spaces into dist/, or into a built site's /space/ (--site).

nodes.title: build-alpha.sh
nodes.summary: Builds the whole Sagebrush site with the space in it, from clean, checks it fits a static host, and copies it to site/public for the Worker that serves space.sagebrush.cloud.
nodes.text: #!/usr/bin/env bash # The whitespace's rough alpha as a static site: the whole Sagebrush site (the Agents page, its workspace, the engine) # with the space viewer at /space/, built into web/dist and copied to space/site/public, the assets of the Worker that # serves https://space.sagebrush.cloud (space/site/cloudflare.config.ts). Run from anywhere in a checkout of # space-prototype; needs node, pnpm and bun (1.3 or later). Nothing is deployed here; then: # space/build-alpha.sh # cd space/site && npm ci && npx cf deploy --dry-run && npx cf deploy set -euo pipefail cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." pnpm install --frozen-lockfile node scripts/wasm-fetch.mjs # the engine's WebAssembly, by its pins pnpm run build # dist/ (TypeScript), which the CLI's bundle and the site need node scripts/build-cli.mjs # build/cli, which web/build.ts checks it is current rm -rf web/dist # (from clean: nothing of an older build is deployed) bun web/build.ts # the site, into web/dist (cd space && npm ci && node build.mjs --site ../web/dist) bun web/csp.ts # web/dist/_headers: COOP/COEP everywhere, each page's CSP, /space/ included # an alpha isn't for search engines printf 'User-agent: *\nDisallow: /\n' > web/dist/robots.txt rm -f web/dist/sitemap.xml # (the Worker's notFoundHandling "404-page": a plain page, no script) printf '\nNot found\nNot found. The Agents page · The space\n' > web/dist/404.html bun web/csp.ts # (again: the 404 page gets its rule) # checks: the parts the alpha needs, and a static host's limits (Cloudflare Pages: 25 MiB a file, 20,000 files) fail() { echo "build-alpha: $*" >&2; exit 1; } grep -q space-frame web/dist/agents/agents.js || fail "the Agents page was built without the space" [ -f web/dist/space/index.html ] && [ -f web/dist/space/space.js ] && [ -f web/dist/space/format.md ] || fail "web/dist/space is incomplete" [ -f web/dist/sagebrush-worker.js ] && [ -f web/dist/sagebrush-notebook.js ] && [ -f web/dist/sagebrush-math.js ] || fail "the engine's scripts are missing" ls web/dist/engine/*/ >/dev/null 2>&1 || fail "web/dist/engine has no engine" grep -q '^/space/\*' web/dist/_headers || fail "_headers has no rule for /space/" grep -q 'Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp' web/dist/_headers || fail "_headers lacks COEP" big=$(find web/dist -type f -size +25M | head -1) [ -z "$big" ] || fail "$big is over 25 MiB" n=$(find web/dist -type f | wc -l) [ "$n" -le 20000 ] || fail "$n files (over 20,000)" # the Worker's assets: web/dist as it is rm -rf space/site/public cp -a web/dist space/site/public cmp -s web/dist/_headers space/site/public/_headers || fail "space/site/public/_headers differs from web/dist's" echo "build-alpha: web/dist and space/site/public ready: $n files, $(du -sh web/dist | cut -f1), commit $(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"

nodes.title: serve.mjs
nodes.summary: A local server for dist/ that sends the cross-origin isolation headers the engine needs and fetches anything else from sagebrush.space (caching it).

nodes.title: site/cloudflare.config.ts
nodes.summary: The Cloudflare Worker for space.sagebrush.cloud: static assets only, no other bindings or secrets, with a route so it wins over the preview Worker's wildcard.

nodes.title: site/src/index.ts
nodes.summary: The Worker's code: anything that isn't a file gets the assets' own answer (their 404 page).

nodes.title: gen-modular.mjs
nodes.summary: Makes the modular-forms space from a Sagebrush checkout: the Rust crates file by file, the Python layers that call them, a note per crate, runnable Sage samples and a 3D plot of the dimensions of spaces of cusp forms.

nodes.title: gen-web-tree.mjs
nodes.summary: Makes the web-tree space: every file under web/ with its first lines, linked by its imports.

nodes.title: gen-demo.mjs
nodes.summary: Makes the demo space: notes, Python, Sage, MATLAB and matplotlib code, and two 3D plots.

nodes.title: gen-self.mjs
nodes.summary: Makes this space: the whitespace's own code, its long files in parts, with summaries and tours.

nodes.title: layout-cli.mjs
nodes.summary: Lays out a space once and saves the positions into it, so it opens the same way every time.

nodes.title: public/format.md
nodes.summary: The space format, written for agents: objects, links, groups, `near`, summaries, tours, what the person selected, and which Sage 3D functions run.
nodes.text:
# The space format (`*.space.json`), for agents

A space is a board in 3D: notes, code with its output, files and 3D plots, placed by their links and groups. In the Sagebrush agents chat, a file you write whose name ends in `.space.json` (with `workspace_write`) opens beside the chat as a 3D space the person can fly through, search, and click. You write the structure, not the geometry: the viewer lays it out.

```json
{
  "format": "sagebrush-space",
  "version": 1,
  "title": "Modular forms in Sagebrush",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "overview", "kind": "note", "title": "Start here", "group": "notes", "text": "# Markdown\n\nWith $\\LaTeX$." },
    { "id": "modsym/lib.rs", "kind": "file", "title": "modsym/src/lib.rs", "group": "modsym", "lang": "rust", "text": "the file's text (or its first 200 lines)", "lines": 812 },
    { "id": "hecke", "kind": "code", "title": "Hecke polynomial", "group": "samples", "lang": "sage", "near": "modsym/lib.rs",
      "text": "M = ModularSymbols(43)\nprint(M.hecke_polynomial(2).factor())", "output": "(x - 3) * (x + 2)^2 * (x^2 - 2)^2" },
    { "id": "dims", "kind": "plot3d", "title": "dim S_k(Γ0(N))", "group": "samples", "lang": "sage",
      "text": "x, y = var('x y')\nplot3d(sin(x)*cos(y), (x,-3,3), (y,-3,3))",
      "surface": { "x": [0, 1, 2], "y": [0, 1], "z": [[0, 1, 0], [1, 2, 1]] } }
  ],
  "edges": [ { "from": "hecke", "to": "modsym/lib.rs" }, { "from": "overview", "to": "hecke" } ],
  "selected": null
}
```

## Objects (`nodes`)

- `id` (required, unique), `kind`, `title`, `text`.
- `kind`:
  - `note`: a thick board; `text` is Markdown, with math.
  - `file`: a source file; `text` is its code, highlighted by `lang` (`rust`, `python`, `typescript`, `javascript`, `json`, `matlab`); `lines` is its length.
  - `code`: code the person can edit and run in the browser; `lang` is the language it runs in: `python`, `sage`, `matlab` or `magma`. Give `output` (text) if you know it; otherwise the person presses Run.
  - `plot3d`: a 3D plot shown as a real object. Give `text` (Sage code making a 3D plot, which runs and replaces the object) and, so something shows before it runs, an optional `surface`: `x` and `y` are the grid's values, and `z[j][i]` is the height over `x[i]`, `y[j]`.
- `group`: objects of a group cluster together, in one color, with the group's name above them from afar. Use groups for directories, crates, modules or topics.
- `near`: another object's id; this one is placed beside it (a sample beside the code it illustrates).
- Don't give `position`: the layout is computed and is the same each time for the same file.

Sage 3D graphics that run in the space (checked Nov 20 2026; each becomes the object): `plot3d`, `parametric_plot3d`, `implicit_plot3d`, `spherical_plot3d`, `cylindrical_plot3d`, `revolution_plot3d`, `sphere`, `cube`, `tetrahedron`, `octahedron`, `icosahedron`, `dodecahedron`, `point3d`, `line3d`, `arrow3d`, `polygon3d`, `text3d`, sums of these (`P + Q`), and the options `color=` (names such as 'seagreen', or 'rainbow' as a colormap), `opacity=`, `mesh=`, `frame=`. Not yet: `list_plot3d`, and `polytopes.X().plot()`.

Notes are Markdown with math (`$...$`, `$$...$$`) typeset by KaTeX; raw HTML is limited to formatting, and pictures from other sites aren't shown.

## What each object is for: `summary`

Give every object a `summary`: one to three sentences on what it is *for* (a file's purpose and its key functions, named as in the code), not a restatement of its text. It is drawn on the object's face, readable from a distance, and at the top of the drawer, so a person learns the shape of the whole before reading any code. Math in `$...$`. For a file, also give `lines` (its length): its slab grows with it.

## Guided tours: `tours`

```json
"tours": [ { "id": "click", "title": "How a click becomes a flight",
  "steps": [ { "node": "picking", "text": "It starts with the mouse: …" }, { "node": "flying", "text": "…" } ] } ]
```

A tour is a path through objects in an order that teaches, each stop with a few sentences of narration: what to notice there, and how it leads to the next. The person picks a tour and goes Next / Back (in a headset too). Three or four tours of four to seven stops are a good start for a codebase. Use real function names.

## Links (`edges`)

`{ "from": id, "to": id }`: imports, calls, "illustrates", "explains". Linked objects are pulled together, and an object's links are listed and clickable when the person reads it.

## What the person selected: `selected`

When the person clicks an object, its `id` is written into the file as `"selected"` (null when nothing is). Read the file with `workspace_read` to see what they are looking at ("this", "the selected one"). Keep `selected` as you read it when you write the file again, and write with the revision you read as `base`: a click since then makes the write refuse, so read again and redo it.

## Tips

- Write the whole space in one `workspace_write` (a few hundred objects are fine). To change it, read it, change the JSON, and write it back: the person's camera and selection stay where they are.
- For a codebase: one `file` object per file (its text, or its first 200 lines) with its `summary` and `lines`, `group` = its directory or crate, an edge per import or `use`, a `note` per directory or crate explaining it, a few runnable `code` samples `near` what they illustrate, and a few `tours`. A long file can be several objects, one per part.

nodes.title: web/agents/page.ts
nodes.summary: The agents chat page (most of it is other work). Its mountSpace shows a .space.json the agent wrote: the space in a frame, sent the file again each time it changes, with the person's selection written back into the file.

tours.title: How a click becomes a flight

steps.text: It starts with the mouse. On a click (a press and release that didn't drag), a ray goes from the camera through the pointer, and the first object it hits is the one you meant.

**openOverlay** first remembers where you are (for Back), then shows the object in the drawer and marks it selected. The selection goes into the address and, in the agents chat, to the page around the space, so the agent can see what you mean by "this".

**flyTo** asks **viewOf** where to look from (in front of the face, or below and in front of a plot) and starts a flight. Each frame, **stepFlight** moves the camera along an arc, so a long flight passes over the space rather than through it.
As you arrive, semantic zoom notices you're close and makes the object's full face texture (the nearest objects first, a few per frame), so the text sharpens as you land.

The face itself: a canvas painted with the title, the summary in its blue band, the first lines, and the output, turned into a texture. Math is drawn as readable text; the drawer next to it has the typeset version.

tours.title: How the agent's file reaches the space

steps.text: The agent learns the format here: objects, links, groups, summaries, tours. It writes a `.space.json` into your workspace with its usual write tool.

The agents chat sees a written `.space.json` and shows it with **mountSpace**: the space page in a frame. It reads the file, sends it to the frame, and sends it again whenever the file changes. Clicks come back the other way and are written into the file as `"selected"`.
Inside the frame (?embed=1) the space waits for the page's message and loads what it's sent. The same file again (the agent rewrote it) keeps your camera and selection, so the space changes in place.
**load** checks the format, makes the objects and links, and lays them out. Positions are never in the file unless saved: the layout is deterministic, so the same file looks the same every time.
One subtlety: what you edited and ran is kept in this browser, tagged with the file text it came from. When the agent rewrites an object, the tag no longer matches and the agent's version wins.
Run (or Run all) calls **runNode**, which takes the object's code and language and hands them to run.js, following progress in the drawer if it's open.
**run** gets an engine for that language (started on first use, one per language) and executes the code in a Web Worker, collecting output, figures and 3D scenes as they arrive.
Back in main.js, the output is kept on the object and its face is redrawn with it. A Sage 3D plot is turned into three.js objects by **sceneObject** and stands on the slab's face.
The result is saved in this browser, so it's still there after a reload, unless the agent has since changed the object.

tours.title: VR: from Enter VR to the panel

steps.text: The Enter VR button appears only if the browser has immersive VR. main.js hands xr.js what it needs: selecting, running, the desktop's views of objects, tours.
Entering puts you where the camera was, facing the same way, on a rig scaled so a slab is about a metre wide. In AR the background is removed, so your room shows.
Every frame: the controllers' rays find what they point at, and the thumbsticks move and turn the rig.
Pulling the trigger on an object flies you to it and opens its panel; on the panel or the wrist menu it presses a button.

The panel is a canvas drawn like a face, but bigger and sharper, with buttons: Run, scroll, Next stop, Close. A page's HTML can't be shown inside a headset, so everything you read in VR is drawn this way.
